walkthroughs.body_html:
Quantities & Units in Mechanics — a core area of A-Level Maths.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Quantities & Units in Mechanics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Quantities & Units in Mechanics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A particle starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 3 seconds. Final velocity is:
options: 12 m/s
7 m/s

mcqs.q: Which SUVAT equation does NOT involve t?
options: v² = u² + 2as
v = u + at
s = ut + ½at²

mcqs.q: What is the reciprocal of the mixed number 2 1/3?
options: -2 1/3, because reciprocal means 'opposite'.
3/7 — first convert to the improper fraction 7/3, then flip it.
It is reflected in the y-axis because of the minus.
1/2 1/3, by flipping each part of the mixed number separately.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between an arithmetic and a geometric sequence?
options: Arithmetic has a constant difference between terms; geometric has a constant ratio.
Arithmetic sequences only use whole numbers and geometric sequences use decimals.
-2 1/3, because reciprocal means 'opposite'.
Arithmetic sequences involve only addition and geometric sequences only multiplication, so 1, 2, 4 is arithmetic.

mcqs.q: How does the graph of y = f(x - 3) compare to y = f(x)?
options: It is translated 3 units to the left because of the minus.
-2 1/3, because reciprocal means 'opposite'.
It is translated 3 units to the right.
It is reflected in the y-axis because of the minus.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Vertical motion under gravity”?
options: Slope = acceleration; area under graph = displacement. Helpful for visualising motion.
Take a = g = 9.8 m/s² downward (or 9.81). Use SUVAT for projectiles, free fall.
Speed is scalar (magnitude of velocity). Velocity is vector — has direction.
For constant acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ((u+v)/2)t. Useful when a is constant.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Variable acceleration”?
options: If a depends on t: v = ∫a dt; s = ∫v dt. Use calculus rather than SUVAT.
Displacement s (vector); velocity v = ds/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt = d²s/dt². All are vectors in 2D/3D.
